questions.stem: Which of the following best defines absolute advantage?
options: The ability to produce more of a good than another country using the same resources
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
The ability to sell a good at a lower price than another country
The ability to produce every good more cheaply than another country
questions.why: Absolute advantage is about output; comparative advantage is about opportunity cost.
whyNot: That is comparative advantage.
Price depends on costs and the exchange rate as well.
That would be absolute advantage in everything, which is possible but not the definition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines comparative advantage?
options: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
The ability to produce more of a good with the same resources
The ability to export more than you import
The ability to produce a good using less labour
questions.why: Trade is mutually beneficial whenever opportunity costs differ, even if one country is worse at producing everything.
whyNot: That is absolute advantage.
That is a trade surplus.
That is one form of absolute advantage.

questions.stem: Country A produces 40 wheat or 20 cloth. What is the opportunity cost of 1 wheat in A?
options: 0.5 cloth
2 cloth
20 cloth
40 cloth
questions.why: 20 / 40 = 0.5 cloth given up per tonne of wheat gained.
whyNot: That is the opportunity cost of 1 cloth in A.
That is total cloth output.
That is total wheat output.

questions.stem: Country B produces 15 wheat or 30 cloth. What is the opportunity cost of 1 cloth in B?
options: 0.5 wheat
2 wheat
15 wheat
30 wheat
questions.why: 15 / 30 = 0.5 wheat given up per metre of cloth gained.
whyNot: That is the opportunity cost of 1 wheat in B.
That is total wheat output.
That is total cloth output.

questions.stem: A gives up 0.5 cloth per wheat and B gives up 2 cloth per wheat. Who has the comparative advantage in wheat?
options: A, because its opportunity cost is lower
B, because its opportunity cost is higher
Neither, because both can produce wheat
Both equally, because they produce the same goods
questions.why: The country with the lower opportunity cost has the comparative advantage.
whyNot: A higher opportunity cost means a comparative disadvantage.
Both can produce it, and one does so at lower opportunity cost.
Their opportunity costs differ, which is the whole point.

questions.stem: Can a country with an absolute disadvantage in both goods still gain from trade?
options: Yes, because it cannot be relatively worse at both, so it has a comparative advantage in one
No, because it produces less of everything
Only if it receives aid to compensate
Only if it imposes a tariff on imports
questions.why: This is the result students most often fail to state, and it is the whole point of the theory.
whyNot: Absolute output levels do not determine the gains from trade.
Aid is unrelated to the gains from specialisation.
A tariff would reduce the gains.

questions.stem: If A gives up 0.5 cloth per wheat and B gives up 2 cloth per wheat, what terms of trade benefit both?
options: Any rate between 0.5 and 2 cloth per wheat
Any rate above 2 cloth per wheat
Any rate below 0.5 cloth per wheat
Only exactly 1 cloth per wheat
questions.why: A will not accept less than it can get at home, and B will not pay more than it can achieve at home, so the range between the two opportunity costs benefits both.
whyNot: B would then be better off producing wheat itself.
A would then be better off producing cloth itself.
Any rate within the range works, not only the midpoint.

questions.stem: What determines how the gains from trade are divided between two countries?
options: Where the terms of trade settle within the mutually beneficial range
Which country has the larger population
Which country has the absolute advantage in both goods
The size of each country's tariffs on the other
questions.why: The theory determines the size of the gain, not its distribution, which is a strong evaluative point.
whyNot: Population does not determine the terms of trade.
Absolute advantage does not determine the division.
Tariffs would reduce the total gain rather than divide it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption of the theory of comparative advantage?
options: Perfect mobility of factors of production within each country
Perfect mobility of factors between countries
Increasing returns to scale
The existence of tariffs on all goods
questions.why: It also assumes no transport costs, constant returns, free trade, perfect knowledge, and ignores externalities.
whyNot: It assumes factors are immobile between countries.
It assumes constant returns to scale.
It assumes free trade.

questions.stem: Which is the most damaging limitation of the theory of comparative advantage?
options: Factors are not perfectly mobile, so specialisation creates structural unemployment during adjustment
Opportunity costs cannot be calculated
Countries never specialise in practice
Total world output falls when countries specialise
questions.why: A textile worker does not become a wheat farmer, and adjustment takes years while the model treats it as instantaneous.
whyNot: They are straightforward to calculate from output data.
Substantial specialisation is observed.
Total output rises, which is the theory's central result.

questions.stem: Why can economies of scale undermine the prediction of comparative advantage?
options: They reinforce an existing advantage, so the first country into an industry can keep it
They eliminate all opportunity costs
They require constant returns to scale
They only apply to primary products
questions.why: The theory assumes constant returns, so increasing returns allow a historical accident to determine the pattern of trade.
whyNot: Opportunity costs remain.
They are the opposite of constant returns.
They apply most strongly in manufacturing.

questions.stem: Why is over-specialisation a cost the static theory does not capture?
options: A country specialising in one or two products is exposed to volatile prices and collapses in demand
Specialisation reduces total output
Specialisation prevents trade
Specialisation raises unit costs
questions.why: The static gain from trade is real; the resulting volatility is a cost the theory ignores, which is why diversification appears in development strategy.
whyNot: It raises total output, which is the point of the theory.
It requires trade rather than preventing it.
Specialisation generally lowers unit costs.

questions.stem: Why is trade based on low environmental standards not a genuine comparative advantage?
options: The environmental cost is an unpriced externality, not a real efficiency
Environmental standards have no effect on costs
Comparative advantage only applies to services
Environmental damage raises the opportunity cost of production
questions.why: The theory ignores externalities, so an apparent cost advantage may simply reflect a cost that has been shifted onto third parties.
whyNot: Standards affect production costs directly.
It applies to all goods and services.
The damage is a cost to society, not to the producer, which is the problem.

questions.stem: Why does comparative advantage change over time?
options: Technology, education, wage growth and exchange rates all shift relative opportunity costs
Governments reassign it by legislation
It changes only when a country joins a trading bloc
It is fixed by natural resource endowments alone
questions.why: A country specialising in today's advantage may find it gone in twenty years, which is a strong evaluative point.
whyNot: It emerges from relative costs, not legislation.
Bloc membership is one influence among many.
Resources matter, and so do skills, capital and technology.

questions.stem: Country A and B each have 100 workers. Before trade each splits them equally; after trade each specialises completely. What is the standard result?
options: World output of both goods rises from the same total resources
World output of one good rises and the other falls by the same amount
World output is unchanged, and it is distributed differently
World output falls because of transition costs
questions.why: Specialisation according to comparative advantage raises total output, and that extra output is the gain from trade.
whyNot: In the standard two-country example both outputs rise.
Total output rises; that is the theory's central result.
The static model has no transition costs, which is one of its limitations.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a production possibility frontier?
options: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with resources fully employed
A curve showing the demand for two goods at different prices
A line showing the terms of trade between two countries
A curve showing the relationship between output and cost
questions.why: Comparative advantage is shown by the relative slope of each country's frontier.
whyNot: That is a demand curve.
That is a trade line, not a frontier.
That is a cost curve.
